posts.note: SXSW 2023 dispatch on a Johnson and Johnson orthopedic robot; one general claim about payment models lagging innovation. Footnote discloses a Spravato KOL advisory relationship.
Open letter about the DEA proposed telehealth prescribing rule after the public health emergency; several implicit and explicit calls about the rule's effects.
Insincere apology to SXSW panels; general claims about psychedelic medicine, regulation and healthcare profitability. Normative 'need to' lines not logged.
Satirical list of panel platitudes ('AI exists!', 'The future is exciting.') not logged as truisms; the sincere DEA comment call to action is logged.
Public billing dispute with Mount Sinai Health System; a GPT-4 drafted complaint letter. Two expectation/demand statements logged as borderline.
Request to Mount Sinai Legal Assistance Clinic to sue Mount Sinai; includes an embedded excerpt of the author's companion ADA post, which is logged.
Website usability rant about Mount Sinai's compliance officer contact page; no forward-looking claims.
Open letter urging a DEA public comment; conditional forecasts of harm if the telehealth rule stands.
Writing advice; one borderline predictive line logged, rest is advice and aphorism.
Reputation management how-to for clinicians; mechanism claims are present tense; one own-activity commitment about Fermata.Health logged.
Live-commentary thread of quotes from a ProPublica event on Cigna batch denials; one quoted third-party claim logged with own_claim false.

Satirical Wizard of Oz parody of a health-tech founder. The Founder's and VC's forecasts (hockey stick growth, disrupting the market) are fictional dialogue mocking founder optimism and do not read as sincere calls; none logged.
Satirical press release from a fictional Association of Genies (an allegory for AI). Its catastrophe warnings are fictional, not the author's sincere expectations; none logged.
LinkedIn analytics essay, mostly retrospective data; one compound takeaway heuristic logged as borderline.
Short video blurb about GPT-4 and ADHD; present-tense claims only.

statements.quote: The Overton Window rarely moves fast, and expecting payment models and accounting methodology to keep up with Healthcare Innovation is unrealistic.
statements.context: SXSW 2023 dispatch praising a Johnson and Johnson orthopedic surgical robot for a realistic go-to-market that fits existing hospital payment and accounting models (staffing cost turned into depreciable capital cost). The author states as a general expectation that payment models and accounting methods will not keep pace with healthcare innovation, and tells psychedelics panels to take note.
statements.note: Borderline: general structural claim that payment models lag innovation; close to a truism, no date or mechanism.

statements.quote: If you think hearing about ADHD is annoying now, imagine all of the people who can’t stop talking about it off their helpful medication —abruptly.
statements.context: Open letter to AI written at SXSW 2023 about the end of the COVID public health emergency and the DEA proposed rule on telehealth prescribing of controlled substances. The author implies that patients with ADHD will be taken off their stimulant medication abruptly when the telehealth flexibilities end.
statements.note: Implicit forecast in a joking aside; the underlying expectation (abrupt loss of ADHD medication access) reads as sincere.

statements.quote: The irony is that very shortly, even this complaint will be indexed by an artificial intelligence product and turned into fodder for a future Generative AI on the topic of regulatory change.
statements.context: Same open letter. The author predicts that his complaint about ChatGPT's limits will soon be ingested by an AI product and used as source material for a future generative AI about regulatory change.
statements.note: Low stakes; about AI indexing of the author's own writing.

statements.quote: And this is something that people with ADHD who aren't going to get their meds will be bad at.
statements.context: Same open letter. The author says people with ADHD will not get their medications under the DEA proposed telehealth rule once the public health emergency ends, and so will be bad at advocating for regulatory change.
statements.note: Implicit forecast embedded in a relative clause; compound with a claim about advocacy ability.

statements.quote: Together, it'll be more accessible in the future.
statements.context: Same open letter. After proposing a 'Generative Advocacy' tool that drafts regulations.gov comments from any rule a user wants changed, the author says that if someone builds it, commenting on regulations will be more accessible in the future.
statements.note: Borderline: conditional on someone building the proposed tool; vague referent.

statements.quote: In short, the current role will be a disaster, so we need to leave comments to let the DEA know by clicking here.
statements.context: Closing of the open letter. The author calls the DEA proposed rule on telehealth prescribing of controlled substances after the public health emergency ('the current role', a typo for rule) a coming disaster and urges readers to file public comments.
statements.note: 'role' is the author's typo for 'rule'. Forecast that the DEA rule as proposed will be a disaster; second clause is a call to action.

statements.quote: Psychedelic medicine would be disruptive!
statements.context: SXSW 2023 'insincere apology' to psychedelics and health tech panels. The author says psychedelic medicine would be disruptive innovation against bad health outcomes, then gives his equation Medicine = science + payment + regulation as the condition for that to happen.
statements.note: Borderline: hypothetical about impact, conditional on science, payment and regulation aligning.

statements.quote: Otherwise, much like Oregon— scams and criminals.
statements.context: Same post. Right after the equation Medicine = science + payment + regulation, the author says that without those elements psychedelics end up as scams and criminal activity, as he says has happened in Oregon.
statements.note: Conditional negative call: psychedelics without payment and regulation become scams and crime; Oregon offered as the current example.

statements.quote: If we don't make the most profits, people will take our good intentions away from us in ways that make more money.
statements.context: Same post, in the list of points behind the author's panel questions. Conditional claim that ethical healthcare ventures that are not the most profitable will be displaced by more profitable actors.
statements.note: Conditional; general claim about healthcare business dynamics, no date.

statements.quote: Thus, the most ethical business in Healthcare will also be the most profitable.
statements.context: Same list. The author concludes that the most ethical healthcare business will also be the most profitable one.
statements.note: General claim, no date; follows from the preceding conditional about profits.

statements.quote: submitting a comment to the DEA is what needs to happen now. Otherwise, psychedelics don’t happen.
statements.context: Short satirical SXSW 2023 post that lists panel platitudes, then gives the author's real point: readers must comment on the DEA proposed telehealth prescribing rule. He asserts that without those comments psychedelics do not happen.
statements.note: Conditional negative call; the first clause is normative, the second clause is the forecast.

statements.quote: The current rule will disrupt care for people with this life-saving treatment.
statements.context: Same post. Suggested text for readers to paste into a DEA public comment: the proposed telehealth controlled-substance rule will disrupt care for patients on life-saving treatment.
statements.note: Template comment the author offers readers; he presents it as his own view.

statements.quote: I expect a response within 14 business days, outlining the steps taken to address my concerns and rectify the situation.
statements.context: Public billing dispute with Mount Sinai Health System over a dermatology visit (CPT 17110) billed above the author's handwritten consent cap of 2 times Medicare. In a complaint letter drafted with ChatGPT-4 and published in the post, the author states he expects a response within 14 business days.
statements.note: Borderline: a demand in a complaint letter more than a prediction; letter drafted with GPT-4 and published by the author.

statements.quote: I expect you will forward this post all appropriate fiduciaries within a 14 day window.
statements.context: Closing line of the same post, in the author's own voice and addressed to Mount Sinai Health System: he expects the post to be forwarded to all appropriate fiduciaries within 14 days.
statements.note: Half demand, half prediction about Mount Sinai's handling of the complaint.

statements.quote: I'll let you know what happens.
statements.context: Post announcing that the author emailed the Mount Sinai Legal Assistance Clinic asking for help to sue Mount Sinai Health System over ADA website noncompliance and overbilling, and that the complaints also went to the New York attorney general. He commits to report the outcome.
statements.note: Own-activity commitment with no directional call; low forecast value.

statements.quote: Generative Compliance is fast. And that scale, they can't keep up.
statements.context: Same post. The author says his GPT-4 assisted complaint filing, which he calls Generative Compliance, is fast, and that at that scale health systems such as Mount Sinai cannot keep up with the complaints. He urges readers to do the same.
statements.note: Claim that institutions will be unable to keep up with AI-generated compliance complaints at scale.

statements.quote: This complaint has already been filed with them as well, and will be with the state. But the trolling for public shame will continue until the health system improves.
statements.context: Embedded preview of the author's companion post about Mount Sinai's ADA non-compliant website, shown inside this post. He says the ADA complaint will also be filed with the state and that his public shaming will continue until the health system improves.
statements.note: Text is an embedded excerpt of the author's own other post; two own-action commitments, no external forecast.

statements.quote: I have it on good authority that the DEA is interested in reading all of our public comments as they were mandated to do by law. And if we get enough of them in, maybe they'll change something.
statements.context: Open letter to the author's wife urging her to file a public comment on the DEA proposed rule for telehealth prescribing of controlled substances (no schedule II without an in-person visit). He says the DEA will read the comments and that enough comments may lead the DEA to change the rule.
statements.note: Conditional hedged call that public comments could change the DEA telehealth rule.

statements.quote: Remember thousands of patients getting buprenorphine by Telehealth for the past three years are going to die if you don't do this.
statements.context: Same open letter. The author warns that if the DEA rule is not changed through public comments, thousands of patients who received buprenorphine by telehealth during the public health emergency will die.
statements.note: Conditional; hyperbolic in tone but sincere about the direction of harm.

statements.quote: And children who need stimulant medication for their ADHD? Also out of luck. And some trans humans? Not going to be able to get testosterone.
statements.context: Same open letter. Further consequences the author expects if the DEA telehealth rule stands as proposed: children with ADHD lose access to stimulant medication and some trans patients cannot get testosterone by telehealth.
statements.note: Compound conditional forecast of access loss under the proposed rule.

statements.quote: That way, when you really have something to say, you'll have the skill set to see it, and a readership who will get to read it.
statements.context: Advice post on writing more, citing Matt Yglesias's daily posting on Slow Boring. The author predicts that frequent writing gives the writer the skill and the readership by the time they have something important to say.
statements.note: Borderline: generic writing advice with a predictive reading; low forecast value.

statements.quote: I will then respond to your review and thank you for that review.
statements.context: Post on online reputation management for clinicians. The author invites readers to review Fermata.Health (his clinic) on Google and commits to respond to and thank each reviewer.
statements.note: Own-activity commitment about the author's clinic; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: there is almost nothing standing in the way of their increasing scale
statements.context: Live-commentary thread on a ProPublica streaming event about Cigna's PxDx batch claim denials signed off by medical directors. The author posts a speaker's line that nothing stands in the way of insurers continuing to increase the scale of such denials.
statements.confidence_phrase: almost nothing standing in the way
statements.note: Quoted third-party statement from the event; the author shares it approvingly ('fire content') but does not restate it in his own voice.

statements.quote: If you write about deeply personal topics about what you're passionate, that's going do well on LinkedIn. If you have content that will provoke a conversation, that will do well on LinkedIn.
statements.context: Analysis of the author's LinkedIn engagement (7.7 percent over the last month) and newsletter growth. In the takeaways list, he generalizes that personal, passion-driven posts and conversation-provoking content will perform well on LinkedIn.
statements.note: Generalized heuristic from the author's own data; borderline forward-looking; low forecast value.
